Title: Effect of a single ultra processed meal on myocardial endothelial function, adenosine mediated effects and cognitive performances
Text:
Effect of a single ultra processed 
meal on myocardial endothelial 
function, adenosine mediated 
effects and cognitive performances
Yousif A. Lucinian1, Christine Gagnon2, Élise Latour2, Virginie Hamel5, Josep Iglesies-Grau2,3, 
Anil Nigam2,3, Francois Harel1, Anna Nozza4, Martin Juneau2,3, Jean-Claude Moubarac5, 
Louis Bherer2,6 & Matthieu Pelletier-Galarneau1
Consumption of ultra-processed foods has been linked to various adverse health effects; however, 
the mechanisms underlying these effects remain poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate 
the impact of a single ultra-processed meal on myocardial blood flow (MBF), measured using positron 
emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT), and its effects on cognitive performance. 
Fourteen healthy adult males were enrolled in a randomized crossover trial, receiving either a 
non-ultra-processed meal (comprising foods from NOVA groups 1 to 3) or an ultra-processed meal 
(comprising foods from NOVA groups 1 to 4) before crossing over to the alternate meal. After each 
meal, rubidium-chloride PET/CT scans were conducted at baseline and during intermediate (80 µg/
kg/min) and high-dose adenosine (140 µg/kg/min). Neuropsychological testing followed each meal. 
MBF and MFR at intermediate-dose adenosine was significantly higher after the ultra-processed 
meal compared to the non-ultra-processed meal (1.62 vs. 1.22 mL/min/g, p = 0.015, and 2.43 vs. 
1.88, p = 0.012, respectively), with a mean relative difference of 40.7%. No significant differences 
were observed between the meals at baseline or high-dose adenosine for both MBF and MFR. When 
considering carry-over and learning effects, overall performance on neuropsychological testing was 
worse following the ultra-processed meal during the first period. In healthy adult males, a single ultra-
processed meal enhanced adenosine-mediated MBF and MFR at intermediate-dose adenosine and was 
associated with potentially reduced cognitive performance compared to a non-ultra-processed meal.

Engineered for cost-effectiveness, extended shelf life, and enhanced palatability, ultra-processed foods (UPF) 
often boast high levels of saturated fats, salt, and added sugar, coupled with a low fiber, vitamin and mineral 
content, elevated energy density, and include various cosmetic additives1,2. The consumption of UPF has 
been associated with a myriad of health problems, including obesity, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia,

hypertension, depression, cardiovascular diseases, various types of cancer, cognitive decline, and dementia3–11. 
Despite these known risks, 50 to 60% of calories consumed by children and adults in North America are from 
UPF12–14. Several hypotheses have been put forward to explain the detrimental effects of UPF, with evidence 
suggesting that the purpose of the processing or the methods themselves, beyond their nutritional composition, 
contribute to the associated health risks15. However, the precise mechanisms underlying the adverse effects of 
ultra-processing remain incompletely understood.
Endothelial dysfunction, recognized for its association with various cardiovascular diseases and metabolic 
syndrome, emerges as a potential mechanism behind the cardiovascular effects of UPF16. Studies have 
demonstrated that a single high-fat meal leads to measurable impairment in endothelial function as measured 
by flow-mediated dilation on brachial ultrasonography as early as 2 h following consumption17–19; however, no 
study evaluated the impact of food processing on myocardial endothelial function. Furthermore, beyond its 
cardiovascular ramifications, endothelial dysfunction has also been shown to impact neurocognitive health, 
revealing correlations with diminished performance in neuropsychological tests assessing executive functions 
and attention20.
The purpose of this randomized crossover study is three-fold. First, we aim at determining whether a 
single ultra-processed meal can lead to alterations in myocardial endothelial function as assessed by positron 
emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT), which allows accurate and reproducible quantification 
of myocardial blood flow (MBF)21,22. Second, we sought to determine whether a single ultra-processed meal 
can enhance the adenosine-induced MBF increase at intermediate adenosine dosage. Third, as an exploratory 
objective, we compared the effects of the two meal types on cognitive performances.
Methods
Study design
Participants were enrolled in a single-center, open, randomized crossover trial during which they were randomly 
assigned to receive 1 of 2 meals and then crossed over to the other meal (Fig. 1). Participants were instructed 
to consume the same non-ultra-processed meal on the evening preceding both experimental visits according to 
provided standardized meal recipes. Participants were also instructed to follow a 12-h fast and to refrain from 
caffeine, alcoholic beverages, and strenuous physical activity for 24 h prior to experimental meal consumption. 
Approximately 60 min following each meal ingestion, neuropsychological testing was conducted. Rubidium 
PET/CT imaging was subsequently performed and analyzed by a certified nuclear medicine specialist blinded to 
all clinical information and randomization group. Each experimental visit was completed in a single day.
Patient population
Adult healthy male patients were recruited at the Montreal Heart Institute and at the Montreal Heart Institute 
Center for Preventive Medicine and Physical Activity (Centre EPIC). Only men were recruited to avoid 
endothelial function variations related to the hormonal cycle23. Other inclusion criteria were age between 18 
and 60 years and absence of cardiovascular symptoms. Exclusion criteria were the presence of cardiovascular 
disease, smoking within the past 12 months, resting blood pressure > 140/60mmHg, renal failure with estimated 
glomerular filtration rate < 90 mL/min/1.73m2, type 1 or 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia (defined as LDL ≥ 3.5 
mmol/L or ratio of total cholesterol/HDL ≥ 5.0), left ventricular ejection fraction < 50%, congenital heart 
disease, body mass index (BMI) > 35  kg/m2, uncontrolled asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
(COPD), known hypersensitivity to adenosine or dipyridamole, second degree Mobitz 2 or third-degree 
atrioventricular block (AVB), resting heart rate < 40 bpm, chronic alcoholism, drug abuse, statin or beta-blocker 
use, claustrophobia, neurocognitive disorder or medication affecting cognition. Eligibility was assessed at a

history and physical examination. Sitting blood pressure, heart rate, waist circumference, body weight and 
body fat percentage (BFP) were measured. Blood work was also completed if it had not been performed in 
the 3 months preceding recruitment. It included serum glucose, lipid profile, serum creatinine, serum insulin, 
C-reactive protein (CRP) and glycated hemoglobin test (HbA1C). Finally, a baseline electrocardiogram (ECG) 
was performed. All experiments were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved 
by the Montreal Heart Institute research ethics board approved the study protocol (#2021–2720). All participants 
provided signed informed consent.
Intervention
The NOVA classification is used to categorize foods based on the type of processing, dividing foods into 4 groups: 
unprocessed or minimally processed foods (NOVA 1), processed culinary ingredients (NOVA 2), processed 
foods (NOVA 3) and ultra-processed foods (NOVA 4)24. The standardized non-ultra-processed meal consisted 
exclusively of foods from NOVA groups 1 to 3 (labeled NOVA 1–3) and was prepared at the hospital kitchen, 
while the ultra-processed meal contained foods from NOVA groups 1 to 4 (labeled NOVA 4) and was prepared 
in a fast-food restaurant chain. Both meals had similar amounts of lipids, carbohydrates, proteins, and calories 
(Table 1). Subjects were instructed to consume the meals provided in their entirety in less than 15 min.
PET imaging
MBF was measured using rubidium-chloride (82Rb) on a Siemens Biograph mCT Flow PET/CT scanner with 
time-of-flight capabilities. Approximately 225 min after each experimental meal, three rubidium PET scans 
were performed: (1) a baseline acquisition; (2) a scan with an intermediate adenosine dose of 80 µg/kg/min 
infused over 6 min; and (3) a scan with a high adenosine dose of 140 µg/kg/min infused over 6 min25,26. There 
was a resting period of at least 10 min between the two adenosine acquisitions. For each scan, an intravenous 
injection of 10 MBq/kg of 82Rb was administered over 30 s using a commercial rubidium generator and elution 
system (Rubyfill, Jubilant Radiopharma, Kirkland, Canada) and simultaneous list-mode PET was acquired over 
a period of 6 min26. For adenosine acquisitions, 82Rb injection and imaging started 3 min after the beginning 
of the adenosine infusion. Prior to the baseline PET acquisition, a low-dose CT scan was performed for 
attenuation correction purposes. Global MBF quantification, encompassing all myocardial regions, was done 
using Corridor4DM (INVIA Medical Imaging Solutions, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA), which relies on one-
tissue-compartment model with flow-dependent extraction correction27 Iterative reconstruction of the rest and 
pharmacological stress acquisitions was performed using the ordered subsets expectation maximization (OSEM) 
algorithm with point spread function (PSF) modeling and time-of-flight (TOF) information, employing 3 
iterations and 21 subsets with the following time frames: 12 × 5 s, 6 × 10 s, 4 × 20 s, and 4 × 40 s. Motion correction 
was performed manually using the tools available in Corridor4DM (INVIA), by visually aligning the dynamic 
frames to the displayed LV contours. When misalignment of tracer activity was observed, rigid translation 
adjustments were applied to individual frames to ensure proper alignment with the myocardial contours. The 
quality of correction was assessed visually by verifying that the tracer activity was symmetrically aligned with the 
left ventricular geometry across the dynamic sequence.
Neuropsychological testing
Paper and pencil neuropsychological tests and tablet-based cognitive tasks were administered following 
each meal consumption in a fixed order. Key components of cognition were assessed: episodic memory (Rey 
Auditory Verbal Learning Test [RAVLT])28 processing speed (Coding of the WAIS-IV, Stroop, Trail Making 
Test A)29–31 and executive functions (Stroop and Verbal Fluency from the D-KEFS, Trail Making Test B)29–32. 
In addition, participants also completed tablet-based executive functions assessments (Neuropeak platform 
developed by Dr. Bherer’s laboratory)33: dual-tasking (divided attention) and n-back (updating and working 
memory).

Randomization
A research assistant conducted block randomization using a MATLAB script to generate random allocation 
before the start of the study. Subsequently, participants were assigned by the research assistant to the appropriate 
intervention according to the predetermined allocation sequence after their recruitment. Investigators 
were blinded to the allocation sequence. By design, the research assistant and participants were not blinded 
to the allocation sequence (meal type/order). The investigators assessing the outcomes (both imaging and 
neuropsychological testing) were blinded to the allocation sequence and interventions.
Statistical analysis
Two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) for crossover study was conducted to compare 
MBF, MFR, glycemia and cognitive performances following the two meals. The analysis included Treatment 
(meal), Period (visit), and Sequence (order of meal) of both visits as fixed effects, and Sequence assignment as a 
random effect. Numbers and percentages are presented for categorical variables. The mean, standard deviation, 
median, and range are presented for continuous variables. A multiple linear regression analysis was performed 
to determine the relationship between clinical variables and the relative difference of MBF at intermediate-
dose adenosine between the meals. Paired t-tests were performed to compare hemodynamic parameters. All 
statistical analyses were two-tailed, and p values of < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. All analyses 
were performed using SPSS (IBM Corp. Released 2020. IBM SPSS Statistics for Macintosh, Version 27.0.1.0. 
Armonk, NY: IBM Corp.) and SAS statistical software version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC. Released 2013.). 
Graphics were produced using GraphPad Prism (GraphPad Software for Windows, Version 10.1.2).
The primary endpoint of this study is MBF at high adenosine dosage. As this is a two-group crossover 
study, the primary endpoint will be measured twice for the same patient, and the correlation between the two 
measurements must be accounted for. We examined correlations ranging from 0.4 to 0.6, which produced 
standard deviations of differences of 0.351 and 0.286, respectively (using a standard deviation of 0.32 for both 
groups)34,35. For our sample size calculation, we used a standard deviation of differences equal to 0.30. Setting the 
significance level at 0.05, a total of 20 patients will allow us to detect a difference of 0.2 mL/min/g (a standardized 
effect size of 0.67) with a power of 80%. Previous studies, however, have demonstrated differences in hyperemic 
blood flow of the order of 0.2–0.7 mL/min/g following various interventions affecting endothelial function35–38. 
(ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06353009, 08/04/2024)
Results
Population characteristics
Out of 17 participants assessed for eligibility between May of 2021 and April of 2023, two were excluded 
because of LDL cholesterol ≥ 3.5 mmol/L. Consent was obtained from all the remaining 15 participants who 
were randomized and imaged. One participant was excluded because of a significant weight loss between 
both experimental visits, resulting in a significant change in the adenosine dosage that was administered. The 
characteristics of the remaining 14 participants are shown in Table 2, with 7/14 participants assigned to each 
meal sequence. The mean age was 31 ± 11 years. The mean waist circumference and BMI were 88 ± 8 cm and 
25.0 ± 2.8 kg/m2, respectively. Baseline screening blood tests and ECG were unremarkable for the 14 participants 
included (Table 2). Recruitment was halted before reaching the target due to significant challenges posed by 
the COVID-19 pandemic, which severely impacted participant enrollment, and prolonged delays that led to 
increased costs.
Hemodynamics
At baseline, heart rate (55 ± 9 vs. 59 ± 6 bpm, p = 0.20), systolic blood pressure (120 ± 12 vs. 114 ± 11 mmHg, 
p = 0.16) and diastolic blood pressure (55 ± 8 vs. 59 ± 7 mmHg, p = 0.18) were not significantly different 
between the NOVA 1–3 and NOVA 4 meals, respectively. There were no statistically significant differences in 
hemodynamic parameters between the first and second experimental visits.
ECG changes during adenosine administration
Two participants developed sinus bradycardia (< 40  bpm), while two others exhibited first-degree AVB. 
Two participants experienced second-degree AVB Mobitz type 2, one following the NOVA 4 meal and the 
other following the NOVA 1–3 meal, both after the administration of high-dose adenosine. All recorded 
bradyarrhythmia resolved spontaneously shortly following the end of the adenosine infusion and did not result 
in hemodynamic instability.
Myocardial blood flow
In all subjects, MBF at maximal pharmacological stress following both experimental meals was within the normal 
range per guidelines (≥ 2.0)39.Two-way crossover ANOVA analysis was carried out to examine the Treatment, 
Period, and Sequence effects on MBF and MFR. All performed analyses had no statistically significant carry-over 
effect (Table 3). MBF at intermediate-dose adenosine was significantly greater after the NOVA 4 meal compared 
to the NOVA 1–3 meal (1.62 vs. 1.22 mL/min/g, F[1, 12] = 8.12, p = 0.015), with a mean relative difference of 
40.7% (Fig. 2). There was no statistically significant difference in MBF at baseline (F[1, 12] = 0.10, p = 0.758) and 
at high-dose adenosine (F[1, 12] = 0.24, p = 0.634) between the two meals. MFR at intermediate-dose adenosine 
was greater after the NOVA 4 meal compared to the NOVA 1–3 meal (2.43 vs. 1.88, F[1, 12] = 8.81, p = 0.012), 
whereas there was no statistically significant difference at high-dose adenosine (F[1, 12] = 0.02, p = 0.887).

For paper-and-pencil tests, repeated-measures ANOVA were conducted with Treatment as within-subject 
variable and Sequence as between-subject variable, to determine potential learning/carry-over effects on the 
tests. First, no main effect of Treatment (meal type) was observed, with the exception for a trend on the Coding 
test, with participants producing more symbols following the NOVA 4 meal (NOVA 1–3, 82.46 ± 5.07 vs. NOVA 
4, 85.47 ± 4.98, F[1,10] = 3.88, p = 0.077). Sequence × Treatment interactions were significant for most tests, 
which suggests different Period effects among both Sequence groups because performances were generally worse 
following the NOVA-4 meal when consumed at Period 1 (Table 4). Performances on paper-and-pencil tests for 
participants from both Sequence groups were compared on their first testing period: NOVA 1–3 for Sequence 1 
Vs NOVA 4 for Sequence 2. No significant differences were observed on either test for this analysis.
For tablet-based tests, there were no significant main effects or interaction effects in reaction time or error 
rate on the N-Back task. In the dual-task, Trial Type (Single-Pure, Single-Mixed and Dual-Mixed) was added as 
a within-subject variable, to analyze specific attentional costs by contrasting the different dual-task conditions 
(Table 5). First, reaction time analyses showed no main effect of Treatment or Sequence, but a significant Sequence 
× Treatment interaction was observed (F[2, 20] = 6.494, p = 0.029). This effect was qualified by a Sequence × 
Treatment X Trial Type interaction (F[2, 20] = 11.094, p < 0.001). Repeated-contrast analyses showed that the 
Sequence × Treatment interaction was significant only when comparing dual-mixed vs. single-mixed trials (F[1, 
10] = 8.71, p = 0.015), which reflects dual-task cost, the cost of coordinating multiple tasks. This interaction was 
due to a larger dual-task cost when the NOVA-4 meal was consumed in the first period (Sequence 2), compared 
to when it was consumed in the second period (Sequence 1) (F[1,10] = 5.59, p = 0.040, Fig. 3).
For errors on the dual-task, a main effect of Treatment was observed (F[1, 10] = 5.492, p = 0.041), showing 
overall a greater percentage of errors following the NOVA 4 meal (1.3%) vs. the NOVA 1–3 meal (0.9%). A 
significant Sequence × Treatment interaction was also observed (F[1,10] = 9.026, p = 0.013). This was reflected by 
a larger Treatment effect in Sequence 2, when NOVA 4 was consumed first (NOVA 4: 1.8% vs. NOVA 1–3: 1.0%) 
than in Sequence 1 (NOVA 4: 0.8% vs. NOVA 1–3: 0.9%) (Fig. 4).
Discussion
In this randomized crossover study, we found that a single ultra-processed meal significantly enhanced MBF at an 
intermediate dose of adenosine compared to a minimally processed meal with matched macronutrient content. 
This suggests that food processing, independent of lipid, carbohydrate, protein, or caloric composition, may 
acutely modulate purinergic signaling. No differences were observed at baseline or under high-dose adenosine, 
consistent with the nonlinear, sigmoid response curve of adenosine receptor activation. At intermediate levels 
of receptor occupancy, where sensitivity to endogenous adenosine fluctuations is greatest, even modest changes 
in adenosine availability or receptor responsiveness—potentially induced by food processing—may lead to

Adenosine is a homeostatic mediator often referred to as a “stress signal,” with extracellular concentrations 
increasing in response to metabolic perturbations, tissue injury, and inflammation. Acutely, adenosine promotes 
vasodilation and exerts protective effects aimed at restoring equilibrium40. Chronically, however, dysregulated

adenosine signaling has been implicated in a range of pathological processes, including fibrosis, metabolic 
syndrome, and chronic inflammation41. The observed enhancement of adenosine-mediated MBF response after 
a UPF meal may reflect a short-term perturbation in purinergic tone that, if sustained or repeatedly triggered, 
could contribute to the pro-inflammatory and cardiometabolic risks associated with UPF consumption.
Cognitive testing, included as an exploratory outcome, revealed modest but intriguing effects. Specifically, 
performance was worse on several cognitive tasks following the ultra-processed meal when it was consumed 
in the first study period, suggesting a Sequence × Treatment interaction. This pattern may reflect an interplay 
between meal type and cognitive readiness or resilience, as well as the influence of practice effects inherent 
in crossover designs. The most consistent effect was observed in tasks requiring divided attention, with 
significantly more errors on the dual-task following the UPF meal. Although these results are preliminary and 
not conclusive due to limited power and potential learning effects, they align with epidemiological studies 
linking higher UPF intake to lower cognitive performance11,42. Mechanistically, adenosine plays a key role in 
regulating neurotransmitter release, including dopamine and glutamate, in brain regions critical for attention 
and executive function43. Dysregulation of adenosinergic signaling has been implicated in cognitive decline44. 
Our findings suggest the possibility that even a single UPF exposure may transiently alter cognitive function via 
purinergic or inflammatory pathways.
Prior studies have reported acute impairments in peripheral endothelial function following meals rich in 
saturated fats, using techniques such as brachial artery ultrasound to assess endothelium-dependent dilation. 
For instance, Lacroix et al. reported reduced reactive hyperemia following an ultra-processed meal but not 
after a Mediterranean-style meal in the same subjects18. However, these studies did not isolate the effect of 
processing per se, nor did they assess myocardial endothelial function directly. In contrast, we used meals with 
matched nutrient profiles and assessed MBF with PET imaging. Our finding that MBF and MFR did not differ 
between meals at high-dose adenosine suggests that nutrient composition, rather than processing method, 
may underlie the endothelial changes observed in earlier studies. This interpretation is supported by literature 
showing endothelial improvements with low-fat diets, lipid-lowering therapies, and exercise conditioning36–38,45. 
Differences may also reflect varying sensitivity of vascular beds; myocardial and peripheral vasculature do not 
necessarily respond in parallel. A study by Scholtens et al.46 using PET-NH₃ imaging found no correlation 
between myocardial and peripheral perfusion reserve, reinforcing the idea that peripheral assessments may not 
fully capture myocardial vascular function.
This study has several limitations. The small sample size limited power to detect small differences in MBF at 
baseline and high adenosine dose, and constrained our ability to draw firm conclusions from the cognitive data, 
especially regarding sequence effects. While the observed increase in MBF at intermediate dose was statistically 
robust, a longer intervention or repeated exposures may be necessary to evaluate cumulative or sustained effects. 
Additionally, we relied on an indirect proxy—MBF under intermediate-dose adenosine—to infer differences 
in endogenous adenosine activity. While pharmacologic adenosine challenge has been used previously (e.g., to 
compare ticagrelor vs. clopidogrel effects on adenosine bioavailability47), direct measurement of endogenous 
adenosine remains technically challenging and is not routinely feasible in clinical studies.
We also explored whether glycemia could account for differences in adenosine signaling, as elevated blood 
glucose has been shown to trigger astrocytic adenosine release in the hypothalamus. However, blood glucose 
levels just prior to PET imaging were only minimally higher after the UPF meal (4.90 ± 0.39 vs. 4.52 ± 0.46 
mmol/L), and this small difference, while statistically significant, is unlikely to explain the observed vascular 
changes. Lastly, this study enrolled only healthy participants, limiting generalizability to populations with 
cardiometabolic disease, in whom purinergic tone and vascular reactivity may already be altered.
Conclusion
In healthy adults, a single ultra-processed meal increased MBF and MFR under intermediate-dose adenosine 
stress, suggesting an acute enhancement of adenosine-mediated vascular effects independent of macronutrient 
content. These findings point to a potential mechanistic link between food processing and purinergic signaling. 
Exploratory cognitive data suggested modest impairments following the ultra-processed meal, particularly in 
attention-related tasks, raising the possibility of short-term neurocognitive effects. While preliminary, these 
results support further investigation into how UPFs may acutely affect vascular and brain function, and whether 
purinergic signaling plays a mediating role in the adverse health outcomes associated with these foods.
